lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Juliane Albieri Calixto | Lesson 10 -- Hiring the Next Designer
lesson.grammar_point: verbs followed by -ing (enjoy, avoid, finish) and verbs followed by to (want, need, decide)

listenings.text: Sure, let me tell you about myself. I'm Alex, and I'm a product designer from Denver. My background is four years in a health app and two years in a payments company. What do I enjoy doing most? Talking to users, and turning research into simple flows. I really enjoy finding the problem behind the problem. My biggest weakness is presenting to big groups. I used to avoid doing it. So last year I decided to give a short talk to my company every month. It's still not easy, but I'm getting better. And why this role? I want to work on products that millions of people use, and I'm interested in learning from a team that works in a trio, like yours.

Hi, it's Ananya. Last year I won an award. This year I lead a team, and I have hired four designers. So, my advice for interviews. First, look at the portfolio before the call, and choose one project to discuss. Don't try to talk about everything. Second, avoid asking questions with yes or no answers. Ask: tell me about a time when... Third, keep listening. The best candidates need time to think. And my biggest red flag? A candidate who never mentions the users. If a designer talks for thirty minutes and never says the word user, I don't need to hear more. After I hire someone, I plan to onboard them in two weeks, with a buddy from the team.

paras: I have interviewed more than two hundred designers, and I still enjoy doing it. Before the interview, I always look at the portfolio, but I avoid judging a candidate by the beautiful screens. I want to understand the thinking. So the first thing I ask is simple: tell me about a problem you solved, from the beginning to the end.

Good candidates enjoy talking about the problem, not only about the solution. They explain their background, the trade-offs and the people they worked with. I also like asking about a weakness. A strong candidate does not pretend to be perfect. She says, for example: I want to improve my presentations, so I decided to present every week to my team.

There are a few red flags. A candidate who keeps talking about tools and never about users. A candidate who refuses to talk about a mistake. And a candidate who finishes the interview without asking a single question. When I decide to hire someone, I plan to mentor that person in the first three months, so I need to know if we can learn from each other. A skill set can grow. Curiosity is much harder to teach.
